newsitem.title: USA: Amid indictments, Columbia/HCA growth outlook darkens.
newsitem.headline: Amid indictments, Columbia/HCA growth outlook darkens.

text.p: As fraud charges were announced against three of its executives, Columbia/HCA Healthcare Corp. Wednesday reported earnings that contained signs the government's continuing investigation was hurting results at America's largest for-profit hospital chain.

The Nashville, Tenn.-based company reported second-quarter net income rose to $412 million, or 62 cents a share, in the quarter, from $364 million, or 54 cents a share, a year earlier -- as Wall Street expected. Sales grew to $5.2 billion from $4.9 billion, the company said.
"It was pretty much in line with what we were looking for," said Howard Capek, health care analyst at CS FirstBoston.

But analysts also said key indicators of future growth were less encouraging. Columbia reported a 6 percent improvement in same-hospital revenues -- above the industry average of 5 percent, but below the company's historic range of 7 percent to 11 percent gains.

"They definitely showed signs of slowing momentum. And this is the first quarter where there's any impact at all (from the federal investigation). So you know it's going to get worse," said Margo Vignola, health care industry analyst at Merrill Lynch.
In connection with a sweeping federal probe, the Justice Department unsealed indictments of three Columbia executives who are charged with health care fraud.

It said a federal grand jury in Florida indicted the executives on five counts alleging conspiracy to submit false cost reports under U.S. heath care programmes, Medicare fraud and making false statements.

Indicted were Jay Jarrell, chief executive of Columbia's southwest Florida division; Michael Neeb, chief financial officer of its northern Florida division, and Robert Whiteside, director of reimbursement at its Nashville, Tenn., headquarters.
Each defendant faces up to 25 years in prison and fines up to $1.25 million if convicted.

They were charged with conspiring to submit false costs reports under Medicare and the military's Civilian Health and Medical Programme on behalf of Fawcett Memorial Hospital in Port Charlotte, Fla., from 1986 until June.

The indictments may heighten the risk that Columbia -- the largest U.S. for-profit hospital firm -- could see nervous insurers, health maintenance organisations and physicians start taking business elsewhere.

"At some point, they start to decide something funny is going on and maybe they'd rather not refer a patient over there" to a Columbia hospital, said one health care industry analyst who asked not to be indentified.

Columbia stock fell 62.5 cents to $33.875 in consolidated late afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was the most actively traded stock, as the market reacted to the earnings news and the indictments.

In addition to announcing earnings, Columbia also said it would not proceed with an agreement announced May 13 to buy a majority interest in America's Health Network, a 24-hour health news cable television channel, from A.H. Belo Corp., based in Dallas. Terms were not disclosed.

The televison venture had been part of a national advertising campaign launched by former Columbia Chairman and Chief Executive Richard Scott, who resigned under fire Friday, along with company President David Vandewater.
The Columbia board of directors was said to be dissatisfied with Scott's handling of the federal investigation and other matters.
Two weeks ago, federal agents raided 35 Columbia facilities in six states and seized files related to laboratory billing, home health care and possibly other issues.
The attorneys general of Texas and Alabama are conducting their own investigations of Columbia.

Named by the board as Scott's successor was Dr. Thomas Frist, the company's former vice chairman. In an interview with Reuters on Tuesday, Frist, 58, said Columbia was discontinuing the national advertising campaign and making many other changes.

He said he hoped to compile a plan to reform Columbia over the next week or so, take it to the Justice Department for review, ask for 90 to 100 days to implement it and then begin efforts to end the investigation that has rocked the company.
